data_section_full_text:
Sample description

Most of our data on audit and nonaudit fees comes from a data base compiled by
Standard & Poors from proxy statements. Our initial sample for years 2000 and
2001 yielded 9,025 firm-years of which 3,415 are from year 2000 and 5,610
from 2001. Panel A of Table 1 gives the details of the sample selection. We exclude
from this initial sample all firms not listed on the three major exchanges (the
American Stock Exchange (AMEX), the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE), and
NASDAQ) and firms that do not have full data in COMPUSTAT. That reduces the
overall sample to 6,284 (2,665 in 2000 and 3,619 in 2001). Further, we exclude all
the firms that are not audited by the Big 5 audit firms for the reasons mentioned
earlier. We also exclude all firms whose operating cash flow is greater (less) than
the book value of total assets in the previous year (negative total assets in previous
year), and also all firms that had negative book values. We do this to ensure the
integrity of the data used in our tests. From the remaining 5,231 firm-years (2,224
in 2000 and 3,007 in 2001), we exclude all the financial institutions (Standard
Industrial Classification (SIC) codes from 6000–6999) because both the audit and

CAR Vol. 24 No. 2 (Summer 2007)

Effects of Auditors’ Nonaudit and Audit Fees on Audit Quality 603

the nonaudit services in these firms are likely to be substantially different from
firms in other industries. Excluding these firms reduced the total sample to 5,095
firm-years (2,166 from year 2000 and 2,929 from year 2001). In order to eliminate
outliers, we use additional filters: (a) firms with missing income or operating cash
flow, PPE, or the data required for computing the change in working capital;
(b) firms with fiscal year-end in September, October, and November (we do not
know for sure whether their reported audit fee in 2001 was their first or second
report, which could potentially create problems of interpretation); and (c) firms
with earnings in the top and bottom 1 percent. This gives us a sample of 4,770
firm-years (1,951 for 2000 and 2,819 for 2001). Further, for our analysis of the
modified Dechow and Dichev 2002 model, we select only the firms for which we
can compute the operating cycle and at least five-year sales data are available to
compute the standard deviation in sales. This gives us a sample of 4,282 firm-years
(1,709 in 2000 and 2,573 in 2001).

Panel B of Table 1 provides the industry breakdown of the (full) sample firms
using the two-digit SIC codes. The top five industry categories in the sample constitute about 50 percent of the sample.

Table 2 gives the descriptive statistics of the variables. Panel A presents the
realized audit and nonaudit fee statistics for the full sample as well as for the two
years separately. In year 2000, the mean audit (nonaudit) fee is $624,520
($1,650,700) and the median audit (nonaudit) fee is $241,000 ($350,000). This distribution is consistent with both Frankel et al. (2002) and Ashbaugh et al. (2003)
(though the fee numbers in our sample are higher because our sample consists of
the larger Big 5 clients only) who also have a subsample from year 2000. Frankel
et al. (2002) report audit (nonaudit) fees with a mean of $511,000 ($1,258,000)
and median of $191,000 ($221,000), whereas Ashbaugh et al. (2003) report audit
(nonaudit) fees with a mean of $514,601 ($1,193,952) and median of $190,000
($197,722). Furthermore, Ashbaugh et al. (2003) report the audit (nonaudit) fees of
firms audited by the Big 5 in their sample as having a mean of $562,420
($1,332,408) and median of $212,000 ($240,100). The substantial difference
between the median and mean values, of both audit and nonaudit fees, suggests
that the distributions are skewed. The median FR in our sample is 1.39 in 2000,
which is higher than the Frankel et al. (2002) median <sup>10</sup> of about 1.04 and the Ashbaugh et al. (2003) median of 1.08 (for the Big 5 sample). The higher FR values
for the Big 5 clients are also documented in Table 3 of Frankel et al. 2002 and
Table 1, Panel A, of Ashbaugh et al. 2003.

Panel A of Table 2 in our paper also shows that the FR (both mean and
median) dropped significantly from year 2000 to year 2001. While audit fees
declined slightly, nonaudit fees declined precipitously over this period. One reason
for the decline of nonaudit fees could be that the decline in stock prices of high
technology firms in year 2000 might have resulted in those firms offering services
at a lower cost. A second reason is that the economic downturn caused the client
firms to scale down discretionary expenditures including nonaudit consulting fees.
The third reason is that in this period, the SEC and other regulatory agencies
started paying more attention to the issue of auditor independence and economic


CAR Vol. 24 No. 2 (Summer 2007)

604 Contemporary Accounting Research


bonding and, in response, firms might have reduced nonaudit services to mitigate
any regulatory attention. All these reasons could have caused the nonaudit fees to
decrease steeply. This decline alerts us to the possibility of systematic differences
in the characteristics of audit and nonaudit fees between the two years. As a result,
we conduct all our tests separately for the two years in addition to the combined
full sample, to ensure that the results are not driven by any systematic differences
between the two years.
